extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists writing proofs, papers, books, and literate programs (graduate students and technical authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and stylistic rules for writing mathematical proofs, papers, books, and literate programs, covering typography, notation, exposition, proof endings, display formulas, and presentation of algorithms and modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid all caps and excessive emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: An entire paper or proof in capital letters is distracting and gives the impression of sustained shouting; the same applies to overuse of boldface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not format whole documents in uppercase or heavy bold; use emphasis sparingly so it does not appear as shouting.

rubrics_metrics.name: End proof marker / box convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Paul Halmos's convention of placing a box at the end of a proof serves the same function as 'Q.E.D.'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use such a box, leave a space between it and the final period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make paragraph breaks clear, especially with displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to make it clear where new paragraphs begin; using displayed formulas can confuse paragraph boundaries unless you are careful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure spacing or textual signposts delineate new paragraphs when displays interrupt text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate notational/typographic conventions for the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Notational or typographic conventions (boldface symbols, arrows over vectors, etc.) are helpful as long as they are appropriate to your audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose conventions that your intended readers will understand; be consistent and avoid exotic notation without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use roman type for ordinal suffixes in indices like 'i+pt'
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a raised 'st' in phrases such as 'the i+pt component', use roman type: 'i+pt' so it's clear you aren't speaking of '1 raised to the power st.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between mathematical superscripts and English ordinal suffixes typographically to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid psychologically bad line breaks and orphaned symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't let the final symbol lie on a line separate from the rest of its sentence; avoid awkward breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nonbreaking spaces (e.g., ~ in TeX) or processor features to tie together symbols and words that should not be separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spelling checkers when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are not naturally great spellers should learn to use spelling checkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run spell-check tools as part of editing to catch misspellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep formulas readable: 'name and conquer' principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid allowing formulas to get so long that they do not format well or are unnecessarily confusing; use the principle of 'name and conquer' to make mathematics readable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce intermediate names/symbols for repeated or complex subexpressions (e.g., replace long parenthesized units by a single symbol) so formula manipulation keeps units intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be stingy with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Overusing quotation marks (e.g., three cute things in quotes) is excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotes only when necessary; avoid decorative or ironic quoting that distracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unnecessary subscripts; use simpler notation when possible (e.g., 'p is an element of P' instead of 'P_i is an element of P').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer lower visual clutter in notation—choose notation that is easy to read and compare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize words like 'Theorem' and 'Lemma' in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to capitalize words like theorem and lemma in titles like Lemma 1 and Theorem 23.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard title capitalization for theorem/lemma names to match academic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sequences of adjacent formulas with no words between; for example, 'Add P k times to c.' is particularly bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert short words or phrases to make the intended operation or relation clear when formulas appear adjacent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before or near where you use them
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to define symbols before you use them (or at least define them very near where you use them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol must be used earlier, provide a local reminder or a concise definition close to the use site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous sentence-opening styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get hung up on one or two styles of sentences (e.g., always starting with 'Thus,' 'Consequently,' 'Therefore,').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence openings for readability; use parallelism when it's the point of the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sentences comprehensible left-to-right (avoid garden paths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to make sentences easily comprehensible from left to right; avoid constructs that temporarily mislead the reader (e.g., 'We prove that (grunt) and (snort) implies (blah)' is misleading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase to make the grammatical subject and predicates clear early (e.g., 'We prove that the two conditions (grunt) and (snort) imply (blah)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Place 'that' according to cadence and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for the use of the word 'that' exist, but final placement must be dictated by cadence and clarity—read your words aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sentence structure by ear; prefer clarity over rigid adherence to abstract rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'shall' cautiously in definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'shall' seems natural for definitions to many mathematical readers, but it is considered formal by younger readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of audience expectations; choose phrasing appropriate for readership (formal vs. conversational tone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in wording to avoid logical ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: If you mean 'not nonincreasing,' don't say 'increasing'; these have different formal meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise terms when logical distinctions matter; avoid informal collapses of double negatives or similar traps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed tenses on the same subject are awkward (e.g., don't mix 'we assume now (grunt), hoping to show' with other tense forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent tense unless there's a clear reason to change; prefer constructions that read smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase proofs by contradiction clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid awkward phrases like 'Assume by contradiction that (blah).'; better: 'The proof that (blah) is by contradiction,' or 'To prove (grunt), let us assume the opposite and see what happens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, reader-friendly phrasing to indicate proof technique rather than clumsy labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a conversational tone with signposts and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone giving signposts and clearly written transition paragraphs provides pleasant reading and motivates proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal remarks, division of proofs into parts, and explicit signposting (e.g., 'first proving (blah) and then proving (grunt)') to guide readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep index order consistent in relations and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving relations, keep indices in the same relative position to avoid confusing the reader (e.g., keep i and j in the same relative position when writing comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a consistent order for indices and vector components; rewrite comparisons rather than swapping positions that the reader must mentally adjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long displayed formulas logically or change notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When long formulas don't fit, break the lines logically or change the math (introduce a new symbol) to improve placement and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should decide how to display complex expressions; consider moving complex parts to separate displays and choose breakpoints (before/after equals sign) appropriately depending on embedded vs displayed formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust sentence punctuation for flow (semicolons vs periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: While editing for flow, sentences can be broken up by changing semicolons to periods or vice versa to control rhythm and tempo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit punctuation deliberately for desired reading pace; break long paragraphs into shorter ones for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve clarity when making stylistic edits
rubrics_metrics.description: While changing sentence structure, ensure any sentences that begin with conjunctions are clear and words like 'it' have unambiguous antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating ambiguous 'it' references or constructions that readers must hunt to resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct hyphens, en-dashes, em-dashes, and minus signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphens, dashes, and minus signs are distinct and should not be used interchangeably; they have different lengths and uses (e.g., 'lines 10-18' uses en-dash).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to typographic differences; use the proper symbol depending on context (ranges, punctuation, math minus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread mathematical content as well as prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofreading you may catch technical errors as well as stylistic errors—think about the mathematics too, not just the prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify mathematical statements, limits, variable domains, and correctness of examples during proofreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use present tense for timeless facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use present tense for facts that remain true; past tense may be used for facts that turned out to be in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer present tense for general truths and theorems; adjust tense when recounting historical or disproven assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitive wording within sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repeating words in a sentence when cleaner synonyms or rephrasing will improve flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace repeated verbs or nouns with alternatives (e.g., 'fill in the entries' instead of repeating 'values').

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit page-number citations for nearby references
rubrics_metrics.description: Give page numbers only for remote references; usually 'using Equation 5.14' is enough without a page number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cluttering references with page numbers unless the reference is distant or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose consistent integral/limit notation based on space
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting limits above and below the integral trades vertical for horizontal space; pick the form depending on formula width and use one form consistently throughout a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on a notation convention for integrals and stick to it across the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and adopt a consistent project-level style
rubrics_metrics.description: Major writing projects each have their own style; you learn what is appropriate as you write more of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep consistency across the work (typography, notation, display conventions, margin annotations) and adopt conventions that fit the project's goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: When long formulas don't fit, consider logical line breaks or changing math
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may change some math (e.g., introduce a new symbol) to make formula placement less jarring; such display choices are a part of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break lines logically; for embedded formulas break after equals sign, for displays consider breaking before equals sign; move a formula to a separate display if that improves comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slash fractions in running text when stacked form is unreadable
rubrics_metrics.description: Overuse of stacked fractions (a over b) can lead to tiny numbers in exponents; copy-editors often convert them to slash form ((1+x)/y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slashed fractions in inline text where readability demands it, and add parentheses as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make exercises unambiguous and redundant where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises have little context, so ambiguity can be especially deadly; carefully chosen redundancy can be important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient information and minimal redundancy to remove ambiguity; this also aids translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit sources for previously published exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to copyright law changes, it is technically necessary to give credit to all previously published exercises; crediting sources is usually sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace history of theorems/exercises where possible; include source citations in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, pithy answers and symbol-starting answers acceptable in exercise solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical guidelines can be relaxed in answers to exercises; quick, pithy answers and answers that start with a symbol are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor style to the exercise context—brevity is fine where context is minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put yourself in the reader's shoes; predict what they expect next
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself what the reader knows and expects to see next; aim for finished versions that read simply and smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restructure exposition so that motivation and explanation occur in the psychologically right order (tell why before stressing significance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid displaying false equations as standalone displays
rubrics_metrics.description: It's a bad idea to display false equations because the reader's eye treats displays as authoritative; instead put them inline as quoted false statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If showing a false equation for illustration, embed it in text like "So the equation '...' is always false!" rather than as a standalone display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous pronoun antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure that the antecedent of any pronoun is clear; revise constructions like multiple 'It is ...' openings if they cause ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague 'it' with explicit nouns when necessary to maintain clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid page breaks in the middle of displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Towards the end of editing ensure you don't have a page break in the middle of a displayed formula; you may need to add text to push the formula to the next page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage page layout so displays remain intact; treat layout problems as a chance to improve exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let proofs follow the same order as definitions and handle cases systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Let proofs follow the same order as definitions; when dealing with several cases, structure proofs accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize proofs to mirror the order in which concepts were defined, making casework clear and predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reference books and dictionaries to resolve usage and register
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult dictionaries and usage guides (OED, American Heritage, Longman, Roget's, Webster's usage) to resolve 'compare to' vs 'compare with', nuances, and spelling conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative references when in doubt about word choice, dialect (British vs American), or usage notes; choose consistent dialect spelling for your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on nationality spelling conventions and be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing for international audiences decide whether to use British or American spelling and be consistent—Americans should use American conventions, British writers British conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing conventions across a single work unless there's a deliberate reason; accept small differences in collaborative notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present algorithms in English pseudocode and follow readable conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting algorithms in a specific programming language can alienate readers; writing algorithms in English (with labeled steps and high-level flow charts) can be more accessible and should follow consistent conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label steps, include parenthetical comments or invariants, and adopt a personal style that is consistent throughout a series; do not ignore the conventions that make the chosen style readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat programs as literature: break into parts and explain twice
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct way to explain a complex thing is to break it into parts and then explain each part twice (informally and formally); this principle underlies literate programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose modules that begin with text (informal explanation) and end with code (formal explanation); use tools (e.g., WEB/TANGLE) to generate both types of output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose consistent perspective in program exposition ('we' vs 'it')
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to describe program behavior as autonomous ('it inserts the element') or as actions of the author/user ('we insert the element'); consistency matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a narrative persona (preferably 'we' according to the author) and keep it consistent across the documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module naming: use imperatives for action modules and descriptors for declarative modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Students used descriptors and imperatives for module names; imperatives (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') work better for action modules, while descriptors should be used for declarative modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the first letter of a module name; prefer concise, readable names and avoid odd capitalization schemes (e.g., FindInNewWords). Use underscore conventions in WEB where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each module should have an informal but clear description
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should contain an informal but clear description of what it actually does—convey an intuition rather than a play-by-play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a high-level account that helps the reader understand the purpose and behavior of the module; avoid low-level step-by-step narration as the main description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep modules short and tractable (about a dozen lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modules that are much too long should be cut into several pieces of more manageable size; a dozen lines is about the right length for a module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break complex functionality into small, focused modules to reflect the philosophy of literate programming and easier comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carrying obsolete conventions into new styles
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing style, avoid carrying excess baggage (e.g., adding comments like 'end {while}' in WEB where it's unnecessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the conventions of the new system and drop outdated practices that were necessary in previous paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use typewriter font for code and specialized numerals (hexadecimal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typewriter type for hexadecimal numbers and code; leave ordinary numeric literals in normal type to help readability and subliminal type-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer monospace/typewriter fonts for code fragments and constants; use 'x' for multiplication in text to avoid typographic asterisk placement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare variables with comments when declared mid-text
rubrics_metrics.description: In WEB you can declare variables anywhere; it's a good idea to add some comment when you do so, even if only cursory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate mid-file declarations to remind readers of their purpose and keep context clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put begins/ends inside called modules rather than in the calling module
rubrics_metrics.description: It's a good habit to put begins and ends inside the called modules rather than in the calling module; mixing conventions can cause bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure code so that module boundaries are clear and matching constructs are locally enclosed; follow consistent bracketing conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use identifiers and variable names that are descriptive and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your variable names are not misleading or too similar to conceptually unrelated variables; choose names that convey meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic variable renaming can improve clarity; prefer descriptive names (e.g., caps_range instead of range) when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concise comments and avoid 'engineerese' in documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive text should avoid 'engineerese' (all conjunctions, no punctuation); documentation must be readable and descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write clear, punctuated prose for documentation; avoid stream-of-consciousness where it hampers comprehension, though a readable enthusiastic tone can be effective if balanced with clarity.
